chapter_theme: Declaring that shame has been given up. The man threatens to ride the palmyra horse, a public humiliation that forces the issue, while the woman, who may not do so, watches her love go into the streets on its own.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar marks 1131-1137 as the man and 1138-1140 as the woman. He reads the man's verses as one argument with her friend: each verse answers an objection she has raised, about shame, manliness, rafts, timing and whether men should endure better than women.

1131.reading: The man says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse.
1131.nuance: ஏமம, 'safeguard', is a surprising word for a public humiliation. The safety he means is pressure: Parimelazhagar explains that the man has given up on the friend's help and intends to get his way as men of old did.

positions.position: உழந்து assumes that he has already enjoyed love and has now lost access to it.
positions.quote: அரியராய மகளிரோடு காமத்தை அனுபவித்துப் பின் அது பெறாது துன்புற்ற ஆடவர்க்கு

positions.position: The word means only striving and suffering because of love, and says nothing of past union.

1132.reading: The man says his body and life, unable to bear it any longer, will mount the palmyra horse, once shame has been put aside.
1132.nuance: He says body and life will do this, and not 'I', as though his person had dissolved into what still suffers. Parimelazhagar adds that with the threat, the man is really looking for the friend to see his desperation and grant his plea quickly.

1133.reading: The man says he once had shame and sound manliness, and today he has the palmyra horse that lovers ride.
1133.nuance: The form is an inventory of property, then and now. Parimelazhagar defines the two lost goods: shame keeps one from base acts, and manliness is not giving way to anything. Notably, it is the man who claims shame here; நாண் in the Kural isn't only a woman's virtue.

1134.reading: The man says that the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness.
1134.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a neat debating context: she objects that shame and manliness are rafts against the flood, and so can't be lost. He concedes that they are rafts, and answers that this flood takes the raft.

1135.reading: The man says that the girl with bangles like a garland has given him the palmyra horse and the anguish of evening.
1135.nuance: Parimelazhagar's explanatory note gives the point: love exists at all times but flowers at evening, and the very name for her implies a young girl, who only echoes her friend. So the man tells the friend that what the girl gave, the friend can take away.

1136.reading: The man says that because of that simple girl his eyes can't close, so even at midnight he will surely think of mounting the palmyra horse.
1136.nuance: Parimelazhagar stresses that பேதை here refers to her foolishness and not her age. Manakkudavar has the friend teasing that he'll forget by morning, and his answer turns his insomnia into a guarantee.

1137.reading: Nothing has greater worth than womanhood, which suffers a sea of desire and doesn't mount the palmyra horse; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.
1137.nuance: The praise also rests on a restriction: she may not take the only remedy he has been boasting about. Who says it changes its force, since from him it is an excuse, and from the friend it is a demand.

positions.position: The man answers the friend's taunt that men ought to endure better: it is the birth of women that has this restraint, and he lacks it.
positions.quote: 'பிறப்பு விசேடத்தால் அவ்வடக்கம் எனக்கு இல்லையாகா நின்றது; நீ அஃது அறிகின்றிலை,' என்பதாம்.

positions.position: The friend tells the man that his beloved suffers just as much, and that women's lot is simply not to ride, to calm his distress.
positions.quote: தலைமகன் ஆற் றாமை நீங்குதற்பொருட்டுத் தோழி கூறியது.

1138.reading: Love doesn't stop to think that they are firm in restraint or deserving of pity, but breaks through secrecy and comes out in public; the speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.
1138.nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a hint under the generalisation: she seems to talk about all women, but means her own love has grown, and that the matter must now be disclosed to the family.

positions.position: The woman speaks, her guarded love having grown; desire isn't afraid of women's firmness, நிறை அரியர்.
positions.quote: 'இவர் நிறையால் நாம் மீதூர்தற்கு அரியர்' என்று அஞ்சுதல் செய்யாது

positions.position: The friend speaks to refuse a daytime meeting because of scandal, and the woman lacks restraint.
positions.quote: இஃது அம்பலம் அலரும் ஆகாவென்று தோழி பகற்குறி மறுத்தது.

1139.reading: The woman says that her love, thinking that not everyone knows, wanders bewildered round the streets.
1139.nuance: Desire is made a separate creature, resentful of her former self-control. She can't ride the horse, so, in effect, her love goes out into the street without her. Parimelazhagar assigns the two verbs to two stages of gossip, அம்பல் and அலர்.

1140.reading: The woman says fools laugh within her sight because they have not suffered as she has.
1140.nuance: Parimelazhagar names the unnamed fools: it is her friend, who has told her family and now teases her. He also reports, and rejects, a reading in which the man says this to the friend, because a man's speech wouldn't fit here at this point in the chapter.

links.note: 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and never give up shame for life. In 1132, the lover sets shame aside to save his body and life. It reverses the ethic exactly, in a book of its own.

For the man, love's flood carries off the raft he had. For the woman in 1164, there is a sea of love and no raft at all. Her situation is worse than his: she has neither the raft nor his palmyra horse.

54 asks what has greater worth than a woman, provided she has the firmness of chastity, using the same words, பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க. 1137 gives the worth a specific content: enduring a sea of desire without a public remedy. The praise comes from a man who is announcing that he won't do the same.

source_issues: 1135: Parimelazhagar's text is truncated. It starts mid-gloss at மாலை யுழக்குந் துயர் with no headnote. Pope's entry also has a stray '11 35'.
1135: Manakkudavar says these seven are the man's (இவை ஏழும் தலைமகன் கூற்று) at the fifth verse of the chapter, which suggests his order or count differs from this one, or that the note is misplaced.
